title: Background to the Abattoir Industry: Abattoir Layout, Systems and Processes;

lessons.title: The red meat industry and the abattoir
lessons.html:
From farm to plate

Beef in South Africa comes from cattle raised on farms and in feedlots. Cattle are sold at auctions or directly, and then taken by truck to an abattoir, where they are slaughtered and turned into carcasses. The carcasses go to butcheries, supermarkets, meat processors and export markets. The abattoir is the link between the farmer and the consumer.

Who is involved

  • Farmers and feedlots that produce the cattle.
  • Transporters who move animals.
  • Abattoir owners and workers: slaughterers, cleaners, supervisors, quality controllers.
  • Meat inspectors who check animals and carcasses so that only safe meat is passed for people to eat.
  • Classifiers who classify carcasses by age and fat.
  • Buyers: wholesalers, butcheries, retailers.

The law

Abattoirs work under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. It says that animals for meat must be slaughtered at a registered abattoir, under hygiene rules, with inspection of animals and meat. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 protects animals from cruelty, and the OHS Act 85 of 1993 protects workers.

Sizes of abattoirs

Abattoirs are graded by how many animals they may slaughter per day. Small rural abattoirs may slaughter only a few cattle a day, while large high-throughput plants slaughter hundreds. The bigger the plant, the more workers there are on each step of the line, and the more specialised each job becomes.

Your place in it

As a beef slaughterer, you do one or more steps on the slaughter line. Every step affects the safety and value of the meat. A careless cut can contaminate a carcass, and a contaminated carcass can make people ill or be condemned, which is a loss for the abattoir and the farmer.

lessons.title: Layout, flow and the slaughter process
lessons.html:
The layout of an abattoir

An abattoir is designed so that the product moves in one direction: from the live animal (dirty) to the clean, chilled carcass. Clean and dirty areas are kept apart so that dirt and germs do not move back onto meat.

AreaWhat happens there
Offloading ramp and lairage (holding pens)Cattle are offloaded, rested, given water and checked (ante-mortem inspection)
Stunning box and bleeding areaCattle are stunned, shackled and bled
Slaughter floor (dressing)Head and feet removed, hide removed (flaying), evisceration, splitting
Offal roomsRed offal and rough offal are cleaned and handled separately
Inspection pointsMeat inspectors check heads, offal and carcasses
ChillersCarcasses are cooled
DispatchCarcasses are loaded into refrigerated trucks
Hide room, by-product and waste areasHides, condemned material and waste are kept apart

The main steps of beef slaughter

  1. Receiving and resting the cattle; ante-mortem inspection.
  2. Stunning so that the animal is unconscious.
  3. Shackling, hoisting and bleeding (sticking).
  4. Removing head and feet.
  5. Flaying (removing the hide).
  6. Evisceration (removing the stomach, intestines and organs).
  7. Splitting the carcass into two sides.
  8. Post-mortem inspection, trimming and washing.
  9. Classification, stamping and weighing.
  10. Chilling and dispatch.

Systems that support the process

Overhead rails move carcasses along the line. Water, steam and hot water supply clean the plant and knife sterilisers. Effluent systems remove blood and wastewater. Record systems trace each carcass back to its owner.

Key points

  • The abattoir links farmers to consumers.
  • The Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 governs abattoirs and meat inspection.
  • Product moves one way, from dirty to clean areas.
  • Main steps: stun, bleed, flay, eviscerate, split, inspect, chill.
  • Every worker's step affects meat safety and value.
